source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 6: Practice Test 1, Practice Test 1 question 58
note: Penetration testing is not named in N10-009; tagged with common security terminology (4.1.4).

stem: Your company is a contractor for the government that regularly works with highly sensitive defense data. To prevent this data from being compromised, the company's datacenter has various special security measures installed. All of the servers have crimped metal tags holding the cases closed. All of the hardware racks are locked in clear-fronted cabinets. All of the cable runs are installed in transparent conduits. These are all examples of which of the following types of physical security measure?
explanation: All of the mechanisms listed are designed to make any attempts to tamper with or physically compromise the hardware devices immediately evident. Therefore, these mechanisms are various forms of tamper detection. Asset tracking is for locating and identifying hardware. Geofencing is a wireless networking technique for limiting access to a network. Port security refers to protection of network switch ports.
whyWrong: Asset tracking locates and identifies hardware rather than revealing tampering.
Geofencing limits network access based on location.
Port security protects network switch ports.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 6: Practice Test 1, Practice Test 1 question 59

stem: You are a consultant working at a client site. The client has supplied you with the SSID and the passphrase for the company's wireless network so that you can connect to it with your laptop. However, you are unable to establish a connection. Which of the following security measures might be preventing you from connecting your laptop to the network?
explanation: MAC filtering takes the form of an access control list (ACL) on the wireless network's access points, listing the MAC addresses of all the devices that are permitted to access the network. If the MAC address of your laptop is not included in the ACL, you will be unable to connect to the network. Geofencing is intended to prevent users outside the office from accessing the network. You are inside, so this should not be the problem. You have been given the passphrase for the network, so you should be able to configure the WPA3 protocol on your laptop. You have been given the SSID of the network, so you should be able to connect by manually entering it, even if the access points are not broadcasting the SSID.
whyWrong: Geofencing blocks users outside a set area, and you are on the client's site.
With the passphrase, your laptop can use WPA3 to connect.
With the SSID, you can enter it by hand even when the broadcast is disabled.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 6: Practice Test 1, Practice Test 1 question 63

stem: ARP poisoning is the deliberate insertion of fraudulent information into the ARP cache stored on computers and switches. Which of the following types of attack can be facilitated by ARP poisoning? (Choose all that apply.)
explanation: By inserting modified entries into a device's ARP cache, an attacker can cause traffic to be diverted from the correct destination to a system controlled by the attacker. This can enable the attacker to intercept traffic intended for another destination. In an on-path attack (also known as a man-in-the-middle attack), the attacker can read the intercepted traffic and even modify it before sending it on to the correct destination. In a session hijacking attack, the attacker can use the intercepted traffic to obtain authentication information, including passwords. Neither of the other two options is facilitated by ARP poisoning. An evil twin is a fraudulent access point on a wireless network. Social engineering is a form of attack in which an innocent user is persuaded by an attacker to provide sensitive information via email or telephone.
whyWrong: Social engineering manipulates people and does not depend on ARP poisoning.
An evil twin is a rogue access point and does not depend on ARP poisoning.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 6: Practice Test 1, Practice Test 1 question 67

stem: Recently, your network has been the target of numerous attack attempts. To gather information about the attackers, you have created a server that is designed to function as an enticing target but that does not provide access to any legitimately sensitive services or information. Which of the following is the term used to describe this technique?
explanation: A honeypot is a computer configured to function as bait for attackers, causing them to waste their time penetrating a resource that provides no significant access. This is also a technique that enables the target to gather information about the attackers. A demilitarized zone (DMZ), also known as a screened subnet or perimeter network, is a network segment on which administrators locate servers that must be accessible from the Internet but that are separated from the internal network by a firewall. A root guard provides protection to switch ports. Spoofing is an attack technique in which an intruder modifies packets to assume the appearance of another user or computer.
whyWrong: Spoofing is an attack that fakes another device's identity.
A DMZ is a network zone for servers that must be reached from the Internet.
Root guard is a switch feature that protects the spanning tree topology.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 6: Practice Test 1, Practice Test 1 question 68

stem: You are a network administrator attempting to use your workstation on the internal network to remotely control a web server called WebServ1 on a screened subnet. However, the remote desktop client software is unable to establish a connection to the server. You can see all the computers on your local network and on the screened subnet. You try using the `ping` utility to test the TCP/IP functionality of WebServ1, and the ping test is successful. You then call your colleague on the same internal network and have her try to connect to WebServ1 using the same remote access tool. She connects to WebServ1 successfully. Which of the following could be the cause of the problem you are experiencing?
options: Blocked TCP/UDP ports on the web server
Incorrect firewall settings on your workstation
Unresponsive service on the web server
explanation: Because your colleague can connect to WebServ1 successfully, the problem is not an unresponsive service or blocked ports on the server. The problem is not a name resolution failure, because you can successfully ping WebServ1 by name. Therefore, of the options listed, the only possible problem must be that the firewall on your workstation is configured to block the remote desktop client's traffic.
whyWrong: Your colleague connects to the server, so its TCP and UDP ports are not blocked.
The ping by name succeeds, so name resolution works.
Your colleague connects to the server, so the service is responding.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 6: Practice Test 1, Practice Test 1 question 73

stem: When geofencing is used as part of a multifactor authentication system, which of the following BEST describes geofencing's role?
explanation: Geofencing is the generic term for a technology that limits access to a network or other resource based on the client's location. Therefore, it is best described as somewhere you are. A finger gesture would be considered something you do, a password something you know, and a smartcard something you have.
whyWrong: Something you do is an action such as a finger gesture.
Something you have is a possession such as a smartcard.
Something you know is a secret such as a password.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 6: Practice Test 1, Practice Test 1 question 95

stem: In most cases, a denial-of-service (DoS) attack refers to a deliberate attempt to overwhelm a server with incoming traffic. However, this is not always the case. Which of the following types of DoS attacks does not involve flooding a server with traffic?
explanation: Although a DoS attack typically involves traffic flooding, any attack that prevents a server from functioning can be called a DoS attack. A permanent DoS attack is one in which the attacker actually damages the target system and prevents it from functioning. This can be a physical attack that actually damages the server hardware, or the attacker can disable the server by altering its software or configuration settings. Flood-based attacks include the distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack, in which the attacker uses hundreds or thousands of computers, controlled by malware and called bots or zombies, to send traffic to a single server or website in an attempt to overwhelm it and prevent it from functioning. An amplified DoS attack is one in which the messages sent by the attacker require an extended amount of processing by the target servers, increasing the burden on them more than simpler messages would. A reflective DoS attack is one in which the attacker sends requests containing the target server's IP address to legitimate servers on the Internet, such as DNS servers, causing them to send a flood of responses that overwhelm the target.
whyWrong: An amplified DoS attack floods the target with messages that need extra processing.
A distributed DoS attack floods the target from many bots or zombies.
A reflective DoS attack floods the target with responses from legitimate servers.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 6: Practice Test 1, Practice Test 1 question 100

stem: Which of the following network devices can provide authentication services for multiple remote access servers using the device's own account database?
explanation: A Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) server can provide authentication, authorization, and accounting services for remote access servers. Network attached storage (NAS) devices, intrusion detection systems (IDSs), and next-generation firewalls (NGFWs) do not provide this type of authentication service.
whyWrong: A NAS device provides file storage, not authentication for remote access servers.
An IDS detects suspicious traffic and does not authenticate users.
An NGFW filters traffic and does not provide this kind of central authentication.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 3

stem: Which element of the CIA triad prevents unauthorized viewing of protected data?
explanation: The confidentiality element of the CIA triad prevents data from being viewed by unauthorized users. Integrity is protection against unauthorized modification of data. Availability provides users with access to the data they need.
whyWrong: Integrity protects data from unauthorized changes.
Availability makes sure users can reach the data they need.
Confidentiality is the element that prevents unauthorized viewing.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 15

stem: You have a laptop that requires you to hold your finger on a scanner pad before you can use it. A device equipped with a fingerprint scanner that is part of a multifactor authentication mechanism is using which of the following types of technology?
explanation: The technology that uses human physical characteristics to authenticate users is called biometrics. Biometric devices can identify users based on fingerprints, retinal patterns, voice prints, and other characteristics.
whyWrong: Tamper detection makes physical tampering with hardware evident.
Hand geometry measures the shape of the hand, not the fingerprint.
Pattern recognition is a general computing technique, not the name of fingerprint authentication.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 27

stem: During a physical security evaluation by an outside contractor, you are asked whether your company uses a fail open or fail closed policy for the datacenter. You do not know what the contractor means. Which of the following physical security mechanisms can either fail close or fail open?
explanation: The terms fail close and fail open refer to the default position of an electric or electronic door lock when there is a power failure. Physical security is often a trade-off with safety, and in the event that an emergency occurs that results in a power outage, whether secured doors are permanently locked or left permanently open is a critical factor. The terms fail closed and fail open do not apply to motion detectors or video cameras. A honeypot is a computer, application, or website configured to lure potential attackers; it is not a physical security mechanism.
whyWrong: Motion detectors sense movement and do not lock or unlock in a power failure.
A honeypot is a decoy system, not a physical security mechanism.
Video cameras record activity and do not lock or unlock in a power failure.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 29

stem: A disgruntled senior associate in the IT department at your company was terminated today and had to be escorted from the building. The IT director has instructed you to disable all of the former employee's accounts, change all network device passwords to which the employee had access, and have the datacenter door locks rekeyed. Which of the following terms BEST describes the director's concern in asking you to do these things?
explanation: The IT director's concern is that the disgruntled senior associate might take advantage of his access to devices and facilities to sabotage the network. When an individual takes advantage of information gathered during their employment, it is called an internal (or insider) threat. An external threat is one originating from a non-employee. Social engineering is a form of attack in which an innocent user is persuaded by an attacker to provide sensitive information via email or telephone. A logic bomb is a code insert placed into a legitimate software product that triggers a malicious event when specific conditions are met. Rogue devices are unauthorized components, such as wireless access points or DHCP servers, planted on a network with nefarious intent.
whyWrong: A logic bomb is one possible tool, but the concern about a former insider's access is broader.
Rogue devices are unauthorized components such as access points or DHCP servers planted on a network.
Social engineering is manipulating users, not the risk posed by a former employee's access.
An external threat comes from someone who never worked for the company.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 30

stem: Which of the following are not examples of multifactor authentication (MFA)? (Choose all that apply.)
options: A system that requires a smartcard and a PIN for authentication
A system that uses an external RADIUS server for authentication
A system that requires two passwords for authentication
A system that requires a password and a retinal scan for authentication
explanation: Multifactor authentication (MFA) combines two or more authentication methods and reduces the likelihood that an intruder would be able to successfully impersonate a user during the authentication process. A password and a retinal scan is an example of a multifactor authentication system. A smartcard and a PIN, which is the equivalent of a password, is an example of multifactor authentication because it requires users to supply something they know and something they have. Multifactor authentication refers to the proofs of identity a system requires, not the number of servers used to implement the system. Therefore, the use of a RADIUS server does not make for an example of multifactor authentication. A system that requires two passwords is not an example of multifactor authentication, because an attacker can compromise two passwords as easily as one. A multifactor authentication system requires two different forms of authentication.
whyWrong: A smartcard and a PIN combine something you have with something you know, so this is MFA.
A password and a retinal scan combine something you know with something you are, so this is MFA.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 32

stem: A user swipes a smartcard through the reader connected to a laptop and then types a password to log on to the system. Which of the following actions is the user performing?
explanation: Authentication is the process of confirming a user's identity. Smartcards and passwords are two of the authentication factors commonly used by network devices. Authorization defines the type of access granted to authenticated users. Accounting and auditing are both methods of tracking and recording a user's activities on a network, such as when a user logged on and how long they remained connected.
whyWrong: Auditing reviews records of user activity after the fact and does not verify identity at logon.
Accounting tracks what a user does and how long they stay connected, not who they are.
Authorization decides what an already authenticated user is allowed to access.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 35

stem: Pulling into your company parking lot at lunchtime, you notice a person without a company parking sticker on his car working at a laptop. You have seen this more than once, and you begin to suspect that unauthorized users are connecting to the company's wireless access point and gaining access to the network. Which of the following are steps you can take to prevent this from happening in the future? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Place the access point in a screened subnet.
explanation: Disabling SSID broadcasting prevents a wireless network from appearing to clients. The clients must specify the SSID to which they want to connect. MAC address filtering is a form of access control list (ACL) that is maintained in the access point and that contains the addresses of devices that are to be permitted to access the network. Both of these mechanisms make it more difficult for unauthorized devices to connect to the access point. The other two options will not help to prevent unauthorized access. Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) is a server that can provide authentication, authorization, and accounting services for remote access servers. Relocating the access point to a screened subnet (or perimeter network) will not resolve the problem.
whyWrong: RADIUS centralizes authentication for remote and wireless users but does not by itself hide the network or block unknown devices from an open access point.
Moving the access point to a screened subnet changes where it sits on the network but does not stop outsiders from connecting to it.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 37

stem: You have configured your company's wireless network to enable a client to authenticate only when the signal strength of their connection exceeds a specified level. Which of the following terms BEST describes the security mechanism provided by this configuration?
explanation: Geofencing is the generic term for a technology that limits access to a network or other resource based on the client's location. In wireless networking, geofencing is intended to prevent unauthorized clients outside the facility from connecting to the network. By allowing only users with strong signals to connect, you help to prevent access to outside users. Local authentication is an application or service that triggers an authentication request to which the user must respond before access is granted. Port security is a method for protecting access to switch ports. Motion detection is a system designed to trigger a notification or alarm when an individual trespasses in a protected area. None of these other options are related to signal strength.
whyWrong: Local authentication checks credentials on the device itself and has nothing to do with signal strength.
Motion detection raises an alarm when someone enters a protected area and does not control wireless access.
Port security restricts which devices can use a switch port and does not measure wireless signal strength.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 43

stem: Social engineering has become an increasingly serious problem on your company network. Which of the following is an effective method for preventing sensitive data from being compromised through social engineering?
options: Install a firewall between the internal network and the Internet.
Install an antivirus software product on all user workstations.
Implement a program of user education and corporate policies.
Use IPsec to encrypt all network traffic.
explanation: Social engineering is the practice of obtaining sensitive data by contacting users and pretending to be someone with a legitimate need for that data. No software or hardware solution can prevent it; the only way is to educate users of the potential dangers and establish policies that inform users what to do when they experience a social engineering attempt. Social engineering is not a virus or other form of malware, so an antivirus product has no effect against it. Social engineering is not implemented in network traffic, so a firewall cannot filter it and IPsec cannot protect against it.
whyWrong: A firewall filters network traffic, but social engineering works by deceiving people rather than through traffic a firewall can block.
Antivirus software detects malware, and social engineering is a deception of people, not malicious code.
IPsec encrypts network traffic, but social engineering tricks people directly and does not depend on reading traffic.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 44

stem: Alice's company has just started working with sensitive government data. To enhance the security of the datacenter, she has implemented some additional security measures. All the servers now have crimped metal tags holding the cases closed. All the hardware racks are locked in clear-fronted cabinets. All the cable runs are installed in transparent conduits. These are all examples of which of the following physical security measures?
explanation: All the mechanisms that Alice has implemented are designed to make any attempts to tamper with or physically compromise the network hardware devices immediately evident. Therefore, this is a form of tamper detection. Asset tracking is for locating and identifying specific hardware components. Geofencing is a wireless networking technique for limiting access to a network based on signal strength. Port security refers to the protection of network switch ports from unauthorized access.
whyWrong: Geofencing limits network access based on a client's location or signal strength.
Port security protects switch ports from unauthorized devices.
Asset tracking locates and identifies hardware components rather than revealing tampering.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 46
note: N10-009 4.1 physical security lists cameras and locks; tamper detection is the closest physical security measure.

stem: To prevent outside users from accessing your wireless network, you configure the access point not to broadcast the network's SSID. However, you later discover that outsiders are still accessing the network. For which of the following reasons is disabling SSID broadcasts a relatively weak method of device hardening?
options: Every access point's SSID is printed on a label on the back of the device.
Attackers have software that can easily guess a network's SSID.
Attackers can capture packets transmitted over the network and read the SSID from them.
Attackers have ways of connecting to the network without the SSID.
explanation: Disabling SSID broadcasts is a way of hiding the presence of a wireless network, but if an intruder knows that a network is there, it is a relatively simple matter to capture packets transmitted by the wireless devices and read the SSID from them. The other options do not explain the weakness of suppressing SSID broadcasts. It is not possible to connect to a wireless network without the SSID. SSIDs are set by the administrator of the access point; they are not printed on the device's label. SSIDs can be discovered relatively easily, but guessing them is no easier than guessing a password.
whyWrong: SSIDs are set by the administrator and are not printed on a label on the access point.
Guessing an SSID is no easier than guessing a password, so this is not why hiding it is weak.
A client cannot join a wireless network without knowing its SSID.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 48

stem: Your supervisor has recently begun using the terms on-boarding and off-boarding, with which you are unfamiliar. With which of the following types of policies are these terms typically associated?
explanation: On-boarding and off-boarding are identity management processes in which users are added or removed from an organization's identity and access management (IAM) system. This grants new users the privileges they need to use the network, modifies their privileges if they change positions, and revokes privileges when they leave the company. On-boarding and off-boarding are not data loss prevention, incident response, or inventory management processes.
whyWrong: Incident response policies cover how to react to security events, not adding or removing user accounts.
Inventory management tracks hardware and software assets, not user identities.
Data loss prevention stops sensitive data from leaving the organization.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 50

stem: Your supervisor wants you to disable all of the ports on the network's switches that are not in use. You tell her that this is not necessary; she wants to know why you think so. Which of the following are valid reasons not to disable unused switch ports? (Choose all that apply.)
options: The unused ports are not patched into wall jacks.
The datacenter is already secured from unauthorized access.
The switch is configured to use a MAC-based access control list.
Leaving some ports enabled facilitates the on-boarding of new users.
explanation: If there is no way for unauthorized people to access the datacenter, then there is no danger of someone plugging a device into a port that is left enabled. If the switch uses an access control list (ACL) that specifies the MAC addresses of systems permitted to connect to it, then there is no need to disable unused ports, because any unknown devices plugged into open ports will not be granted access to the network. The other two options are not valid reasons. Ports that are not patched in can still be compromised at the switch location. Enabling ports is not difficult for authorized administrators, so accommodating new users is not a valid reason for leaving the ports enabled.
whyWrong: Ports that are not patched to wall jacks can still be used by someone with access to the switch itself.
Authorized administrators can enable ports easily, so new users are not a valid reason to leave them enabled.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 52

stem: Which of the following are security mechanisms that fall into the category of deception technologies?
explanation: A honeypot or honeynet is a computer or network configured to function as deceptive bait for potential attackers, causing them to waste their time and effort penetrating a resource that provides no significant access or advantage. The other three options are not deception technologies. A root guard provides protection to switch ports by affecting the behavior of the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) to enforce the selection of root bridge ports on a switched network. A screened subnet (also called a perimeter network) is the part of a network where administrators locate servers that must be accessible from the Internet, such as email and web servers. Geofencing is a security mechanism that prevents unauthorized clients outside the facility from connecting to the network.
whyWrong: Root guard is a spanning tree feature that protects the root bridge selection on switch ports.
A screened subnet is a perimeter network for servers that must be reachable from the Internet.
Geofencing limits network access based on the client's location.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 53

stem: Which of the following network devices can employ access control lists (ACLs) to restrict access? (Choose all that apply.)
explanation: ACLs restrict access to network devices by filtering user names, MAC addresses, IP addresses, or other criteria. Routers, servers, switches, and wireless access points all can use ACLs to control access to them. Hubs are purely Physical layer devices that relay electrical or optical signals. They have no access control mechanisms.
whyWrong: Hubs are Physical layer devices that only repeat signals and have no access control features.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 54

stem: Which of the following statements about DHCP snooping are true? (Choose all that apply.)
options: DHCP snooping is implemented in network switches.
DHCP snooping prevents DNS cache poisoning.
DHCP snooping detects rogue DHCP servers.
DHCP snooping drops DHCP messages arriving over the incorrect port.
explanation: DHCP snooping is a feature found in some network switches that prevents rogue DHCP servers from assigning IP addresses to clients. It can also detect when DHCP release or decline messages arrive over a port other than the one on which the DHCP transaction originated. Although DHCP snooping can prevent DHCP clients from being assigned an incorrect IP address, it does not directly prevent the poisoning of DNS server caches with erroneous information.
whyWrong: DHCP snooping protects DHCP address assignment and does not stop the poisoning of DNS server caches.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 56

stem: Virtual LAN (VLAN) hopping is a type of attack directed at network switches. Which of the following BEST describes how VLAN hopping is a potential threat?
options: VLAN hopping enables an attacker to access different VLANs using 802.1q spoofing.
VLAN hopping enables an attacker to scramble a switch's patch panel connections.
VLAN hopping enables an attacker to change the native VLAN on a switch.
VLAN hopping enables an attacker to rename the default VLAN on a switch.
explanation: VLAN hopping is a method for sending false commands to switches to transfer a port from one VLAN to another. This can enable the attacker to connect his or her device to a potentially sensitive VLAN. VLAN hopping does not modify the switch's patch panel connections, only its VLAN assignments. It is not possible to rename a switch's default VLAN. VLAN hopping does not enable an attacker to change a switch's native VLAN.
whyWrong: VLAN hopping changes VLAN assignments in software and cannot alter physical patch panel connections.
VLAN hopping lets an attacker reach other VLANs but does not let them change the switch's native VLAN.
The default VLAN of a switch cannot be renamed, by an attacker or anyone else.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 63

stem: Which of the following attack types does not specifically target wireless network clients?
explanation: A logic bomb is a code insert placed into a legitimate software product that triggers a malicious event when specific conditions are met. Therefore, it can affect both wired and wireless clients. The other options are all attacks directed at wireless networks. Deauthentication is a type of denial-of-service attack in which the attacker targets a wireless client by sending a deauthentication frame that causes the client to be disconnected from the network. The object of the attack is often to compel the client to connect to a rogue access point called an evil twin. An evil twin is a fraudulent access point on a wireless network that mimics the SSID of a legitimate access point, in the hope of luring in users. A rogue AP is a wireless access point that has been connected to a network by an intruder in the hope of luring users into connecting to it.
whyWrong: A deauthentication attack sends forged frames that disconnect wireless clients from an access point.
An evil twin is a fake access point that copies a legitimate SSID to lure wireless clients.
A rogue AP is an unauthorized access point placed on a network to attract wireless clients.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 67

stem: You have just finished installing a web server farm on your company's network, along with a router to create a screened subnet (perimeter network) on which the web servers are located. However, you now cannot access the web servers from your workstation on the internal network. Which of the following is not one of the tasks you will have to complete before you can access the screened subnet from the internal network?
explanation: MAC addresses are hard-coded into network interface adapters and are not easily changeable. There is also no need to change them for this purpose. First, you will have to change IP addresses of the web servers. This is because the computers on the other side of the router, on the screened subnet, must use an IP network address that is different from the internal network's address. Next, you will have to change the default gateway address setting on the internal network computers to the address of the router on the internal network so that traffic can be forwarded to the screened subnet. Finally, you will have to update the resource records on your DNS server to reflect the IP address changes.
whyWrong: The web servers on the screened subnet need IP addresses on a different network from the internal one, so the addresses must change.
The DNS records must be updated so that names resolve to the web servers' new IP addresses.
Internal computers need a default gateway that can forward traffic through the router to the screened subnet.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 7: Practice Test 2, Practice Test 2 question 81

stem: Which two encryption protocols might be used to secure transmissions for email services?
explanation: SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) and its successor TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypt data in transit for many application protocols, including email protocols such as SMTP, POP3, and IMAP. Secure email versions of these protocols use SSL/TLS to protect messages and credentials as they cross the network. TLS has replaced SSL, which is now considered insecure.
whyWrong: HTTP is unencrypted, and HTTPS secures web traffic rather than email services.
FTP and SFTP are file transfer protocols, and FTP is not encrypted at all.
SSH secures remote command-line sessions and RDP provides remote desktop access, not email encryption.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 1: Introduction to Networking, Review Questions question 4

stem: In the event of a fire, a failure policy that ensures all doors remain unlocked is called a __________ policy.
explanation: A fail-open (fail-safe) policy makes a security system allow access when it fails, so doors default to unlocked during a fire or power failure. This lets people leave the building safely and firefighters enter, even though it adds a security risk. A fail-close (fail-secure) policy does the opposite and keeps doors locked during a failure.
whyWrong: Power-off is not a name for a security failure policy.
A fail-close policy keeps doors locked when the system fails, which is the opposite of what is described.
Shutdown is not a name for a security failure policy.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 1: Introduction to Networking, Review Questions question 10
note: Fail-open and fail-close policies are not named in N10-009; they relate to door locks under physical security.

stem: Which component of the CIA triad can be ensured when data is encrypted by a private key and decrypted by the matching public key?
explanation: Public key encryption can ensure data integrity, as the sender’s public key will only work to decrypt data encrypted with the sender’s private key if the data has not been tampered with. Encrypting data with a public key and decrypting with the matching private key ensures confidentiality, as only the intended recipient (the owner of the keys) can use the private key to decrypt data encrypted with their corresponding public key. Availability refers to the data being available to the intended recipient when needed, meaning the sender is accountable for successful delivery of the data.
whyWrong: Confidentiality is ensured when data is encrypted with the recipient's public key and decrypted with their private key.
Availability means the data can be reached by the intended recipient when it is needed.
Accountability is not one of the three components of the CIA triad.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 4: Protocols, Self-Check question 4

stem: Which encryption benchmark ensures data is not modified after it’s transmitted and before it’s received?
explanation: Integrity ensures that data has not been modified between the time it is sent and the time it is received. Techniques such as hashing and digital signatures let the receiver check that the data arrived unchanged. Integrity is one of the three parts of the CIA triad, with confidentiality and availability.
whyWrong: Confidentiality keeps data from being read by unauthorized people but does not detect changes.
Availability means data and resources can be reached by authorized users when needed.
Symmetric describes an encryption method that uses one shared key, not a security benchmark of the CIA triad.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 4: Protocols, Review Questions question 6

stem: When surfing online, you get some strange data on an apparently secure website, and you realize you need to check the legitimacy of the site. What entity issues digital certificates for websites?
explanation: A CA (certificate authority) is a trusted organization that issues and signs digital certificates for websites. The certificate binds the site's public key to its identity, so a browser can check that the site is legitimate. CAs are part of the PKI (public key infrastructure) that makes this trust possible.
whyWrong: A registrar registers domain names and does not issue digital certificates.
PKI is the whole system of keys, certificates, and authorities, not the single entity that issues certificates.
Active Directory is a Windows directory service for users and computers, not a public certificate issuer.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 4: Protocols, Scenario-Based Questions question 2

stem: Which offboarding policy can protect proprietary corporate information if a smartphone is lost?
explanation: The ability to perform a remote wipe is part of an offboarding policy that clears a device of important information, permissions, and apps without having physical access to the device. Onboarding gives the device trusted access to certain portions of the network. An onboarding agent might also scan the device for any needed OS or security updates, required security settings (such as timeouts or sign-in requirements), and any existing malware. A site survey assesses client requirements, facility characteristics, and coverage areas when determining the best placement for APs in a wireless network.
whyWrong: Trusted access is granted to a device during onboarding, not used to protect data when it is lost.
OS update requirements are checked during onboarding and do not erase data from a lost device.
A site survey plans access point placement for a wireless network.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking, Self-Check question 6

stem: You’ve just completed a survey of the wireless signals traversing the airspace in your company’s vicinity, and you’ve found an unauthorized AP with a very strong signal near the middle of the 100-acre campus. Its SSID is broadcasting the name of a smartphone model. What kind of threat do you need to report to your boss?
explanation: A rogue AP is an unauthorized access point within range of the network, often set up to lure users into connecting to it. An unknown AP with a strong signal in the middle of the campus is a threat that should be reported and removed. A wireless survey that finds unexpected SSIDs is a common way to detect rogue access points.
whyWrong: Skimming is the theft of card data with a hidden card reader.
War driving is driving around to find and map wireless networks, not an access point placed on the campus.
A hidden node is a wireless client that other clients cannot hear, which causes collisions rather than a security threat.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking, Scenario-Based Questions question 2

stem: You just settled in for some study time at the local coffee shop, and you pause long enough to connect your smartphone to the Wi-Fi so you can listen to some music while you study. As you’re about to sign in, you realize that you clicked an SSID called “Free Coffee and Internet.” What kind of security trap did you almost fall for?
explanation: An evil twin is a rogue access point with an attractive or familiar SSID that lures users into connecting to it. Once a user connects, the attacker can capture the user's traffic and credentials. Users should confirm the real SSID of a public hotspot before they connect.
whyWrong: Interference is unwanted signal noise that degrades wireless connections, not a trap set by an attacker.
A captive portal is a legitimate sign-in page that a hotspot shows before it grants access.
A brute force attack tries many passwords or keys until one works.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking, Scenario-Based Questions question 3

stem: What information does the switchport port-security command use to restrict access to a switch’s interface?
explanation: Port security restricts a switch interface to the MAC addresses that are allowed to use it. The switch learns or is given the permitted MAC addresses and can shut down or restrict the port when a different address appears. This stops unknown devices from connecting through an open port.
whyWrong: The port number identifies the interface being protected, not the devices allowed to use it.
Switch port security works at Layer 2 and does not filter by IP address.
A broadcast address is a destination for all hosts and cannot identify an allowed device.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture, Review Questions question 4

stem: Which of the following statements describes a SCADA system?
explanation: SCADA systems use a centralized architecture for control of devices within a closed environment. IIoT systems, by contrast, are designed for Internet exposure and focus on collecting massive amounts of data for detailed analysis.
whyWrong: SCADA systems use a centralized architecture, not a decentralized one.
Internet exposure is a feature of IIoT systems, while SCADA systems are kept in a closed environment.
Collecting massive amounts of data for analysis describes IIoT systems rather than SCADA.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 8: Network Segmentation, Self-Check question 2

stem: An attacker configures a VLAN frame with two tags instead of just one. The first tag directs the frame to the authorized VLAN. After the frame enters the first VLAN, the switch appropriately removes the tag, then discovers the next tag, and sends the frame along to a protected VLAN, which the attacker is not authorized to access. What kind of attack is this?
explanation: This is VLAN hopping by double tagging. The attacker adds two VLAN tags so that the first switch removes the outer tag and forwards the frame using the inner tag to a VLAN the attacker cannot reach. Switch spoofing is the other form of VLAN hopping, in which the attacker's device pretends to be a switch to form a trunk.
whyWrong: Port tagging is the normal use of VLAN tags on trunk ports, not an attack.
Switch spoofing is a VLAN hopping method in which a device pretends to be a switch to form a trunk, not one that uses two tags.
VLAN isolation is a defense that keeps VLAN traffic separate, not an attack.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 8: Network Segmentation, Scenario-Based Questions question 2

stem: Which policy ensures messages are discarded when they don’t match a specific firewall rule?
explanation: Implicit deny means that any traffic that does not match a rule is discarded by default. Firewalls and ACLs usually end with an unwritten deny rule that applies when no earlier rule matches. Explicit rules are written to allow or deny specific traffic.
whyWrong: Implicit allow would pass traffic that matches no rule, which is the opposite of what is described.
An explicit deny rule blocks traffic that matches that specific rule, not traffic that matches no rule.
An explicit allow rule permits traffic that matches it.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking, Review Questions question 7

stem: Which ACL rule will prevent pings from a host at 192.168.2.100?
explanation: Ping uses ICMP, so the rule must deny ICMP traffic. To stop pings from the host, the host 192.168.2.100 must be the source address and any address the destination. In an extended ACL the source comes before the destination.
whyWrong: This rule permits ICMP traffic to the host instead of blocking pings from it.
This rule denies TCP traffic, but ping uses ICMP.
This rule blocks pings sent to the host, not pings sent from it.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking, Review Questions question 8

stem: What is the MOST LIKELY cause of a firewall blocking traffic that should be allowed?
explanation: A firewall that blocks traffic it should allow is most often caused by a misconfigured rule, such as a wrong port, address, or rule order. Because rules are processed in order, a broad deny rule placed above an allow rule can block the wanted traffic. Checking the rule set is the first thing to do before suspecting hardware.
whyWrong: A failed device usually stops all traffic or fails in a set way, which is less likely than a rule error.
Rule exceptions are deliberate entries that allow specific traffic, not a cause of blocked traffic.
Packets are not configured on a firewall, so packet misconfiguration is not a firewall cause.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking, Review Questions question 9

stem: The ability to insert code into a database field labeled “Name” is an example of a(n) _________________.
explanation: A weakness of a system, process, or architecture that could lead to compromised information or unauthorized access is known as a vulnerability. The act of taking advantage of a vulnerability is known as an exploit or attack. Unauthorized access or use of sensitive data is called a data breach.
whyWrong: An attack is the act of using a weakness, not the weakness itself.
A breach is unauthorized access to or use of sensitive data.
An exploit is the act of taking advantage of a vulnerability.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 10: Risk Management, Self-Check question 1

stem: Which of the following social engineering attack types MOST LIKELY requires that the attacker have existing knowledge about the victim?
explanation: Phishing is communication that appears to come from a legitimate source and requests access or authentication information; to be most effective, phishing typically must build on pre-existing knowledge about the victim, such as knowing the victim’s name, the name of their boss, companies they do business with, or similar information. Tailgating, piggybacking, and shoulder surfing are more transient in nature and don’t require any existing knowledge about the victim to be successful.
whyWrong: Tailgating follows an authorized person through a secured door and needs no knowledge about the victim.
Shoulder surfing watches someone enter information and needs no prior knowledge about the victim.
Piggybacking enters a secured area with an authorized person's consent and needs no prior knowledge about the victim.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 10: Risk Management, Self-Check question 2

stem: You’re playing a game on your Xbox when you suddenly get bumped off your Wi-Fi network. You reconnect and start playing, then get bumped off again. What type of attack is MOST LIKELY the cause?
explanation: In a deauth (deauthentication) attack, the attacker sends faked deauthentication frames to the AP, the client, or both (or as a broadcast to the whole wireless network) to trigger the deauthentication process and knock one or more clients off the wireless network. An on-path attack, also called an MitM (man-in-the-middle) attack, relies on intercepted transmissions. In a well-known exploit called FTP bounce, hackers take advantage of the insecure FTP protocol. DDoS (distributed DoS) attacks are orchestrated through many sources to prevent legitimate users from accessing normal network resources.
whyWrong: An on-path attack intercepts traffic between two parties rather than knocking a client off the network.
FTP bounce abuses the insecure FTP protocol and does not disconnect Wi-Fi clients.
A DDoS attack floods a target from many sources rather than sending deauthentication frames to one client.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 10: Risk Management, Self-Check question 3

stem: What is the FIRST step in improving network security?
options: Determine which resources might be harmed.
Develop plans for responding to threats.
explanation: Before spending time and money changing your network security, first identify your network's current security risks. The next steps include determining which resources might be harmed if each risk were exploited, developing plans to respond to threats, and documenting next steps.
whyWrong: Documenting next steps comes at the end, after the risks and responses are known.
Deciding which resources might be harmed comes after the risks have been identified.
Response plans are developed after the risks and the resources they affect are known.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 10: Risk Management, Self-Check question 4

stem: Which assessment type would MOST LIKELY discover a security risk related to employee on-boarding?
explanation: A process assessment is used to identify business processes and evaluate risks related to those processes, such as a security risk in an existing employee on-boarding process. A vendor risk assessment (also called a third-party risk assessment) evaluates security and compliance risks related to suppliers and vendors a company does business with. A threat assessment identifies specific security threats to the network and related risk factors. A posture assessment is a thorough examination of each aspect of the network to determine how it might be compromised.
whyWrong: A vendor risk assessment evaluates the risks of suppliers and vendors, not internal processes.
A threat assessment identifies specific threats to the network and their risk factors.
A posture assessment examines every aspect of the network for ways it might be compromised.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 10: Risk Management, Self-Check question 5
note: N10-009 does not list assessment types; audits and compliance is the closest topic.

stem: Which type of DoS attack orchestrates an attack bounced off uninfected computers?
explanation: A DRDoS (distributed reflection DoS) attack sends requests with the victim's spoofed address to many uninfected computers. Those computers send their replies to the victim, so the attack is bounced off them. Amplified DRDoS attacks use requests that produce much larger responses.
whyWrong: FTP bounce abuses the insecure FTP protocol to send traffic through an FTP server, not through many uninfected computers.
Ransomware encrypts or locks a victim's data and demands payment.
A PDoS attack permanently damages a device, for example by corrupting its firmware.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 10: Risk Management, Review Questions question 1

stem: What type of attack relies on spoofing?
explanation: A deauth attack relies on spoofing: the attacker sends forged deauthentication frames that appear to come from the access point or the client. The frames disconnect clients from the wireless network, which is a form of denial of service. Attackers often use it to push clients toward an evil twin access point.
whyWrong: A friendly DoS attack is an unintentional flood of legitimate traffic, so no spoofing is involved.
Tailgating is a physical social engineering attack that follows someone through a secured door.
Pen testing is an authorized simulated attack used to find weaknesses, not an attack type that relies on spoofing.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 10: Risk Management, Review Questions question 3

stem: Which device would allow an attacker to make network clients use an illegitimate default gateway?
explanation: A rogue DHCP server can hand out IP settings that include an illegitimate default gateway controlled by the attacker. Clients then send their traffic through the attacker's device, which allows an on-path attack. DHCP snooping on switches helps stop rogue DHCP servers.
whyWrong: A cipher lock is a physical lock that opens with a code and has no effect on network settings.
A TAP copies traffic for monitoring and does not assign a default gateway to clients.
A honeypot is a decoy system that lures attackers and does not configure clients.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 10: Risk Management, Review Questions question 4

stem: Leading up to the year 2000, many people expected computer systems the world over to fail when clocks turned the date to January 1, 2000. What type of threat was this?
explanation: A logic bomb is code, or a bug in code, that activates when a certain condition is met, such as a specific date. The expected Y2K failures were tied to a date, so they behaved like time-dependent logic bombs. Logic bombs can stay dormant until their trigger condition arrives.
whyWrong: Ransomware locks or encrypts data and demands payment, and it is not triggered by a calendar date.
A virus attaches to files and spreads when they are run, not when a date arrives.
A worm spreads by itself across a network and is not triggered by a date.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 10: Risk Management, Review Questions question 5

stem: Which of the following attack simulations detect vulnerabilities and attempt to exploit them? Choose TWO.
explanation: A pen test (penetration test) is an authorized attack that finds vulnerabilities and then tries to exploit them. A red team–blue team exercise also simulates an attack, with the red team attacking and the blue team defending. A vulnerability assessment and a security audit find and report weaknesses but do not try to exploit them.
whyWrong: A vulnerability assessment finds and reports weaknesses but does not try to exploit them.
A security audit reviews the organization's security against a standard and does not attempt attacks.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 10: Risk Management, Review Questions question 6
note: N10-009 does not list attack simulations; they relate to finding vulnerabilities and exploits.

stem: What is the difference between a vulnerability and an exploit?
options: A vulnerability takes advantage of an exploit.
A vulnerability is the likelihood that a risk will be exploited.
An exploit takes advantage of a vulnerability.
A risk is the likelihood that a vulnerability will be exploited.
explanation: A vulnerability is a weakness in a system, process, or design. An exploit is the act of taking advantage of that weakness, for example by running code that uses it. Risk is the likelihood that a vulnerability will be exploited.
whyWrong: The relationship is reversed, because an exploit takes advantage of a vulnerability.
The likelihood that a weakness will be exploited is a risk, not a vulnerability.
This statement defines risk correctly but does not explain the difference between a vulnerability and an exploit.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 10: Risk Management, Review Questions question 7

stem: What is the FIRST phase of the social engineering attack cycle?
explanation: Research is Phase 1 of the social engineering attack cycle, and it often takes the most time. The attacker collects public information and seemingly harmless details about the target. In Phase 2 the attacker uses those details to build trust and gain access to more private information.
whyWrong: Quid pro quo is a type of social engineering attack that offers something in exchange, not the first phase of the cycle.
Phishing is a type of social engineering attack, not the first phase of the attack cycle.
Building trust is Phase 2, after the attacker has done research.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 10: Risk Management, Review Questions question 8

stem: What characteristic of ARP makes it particularly vulnerable to being used in a DoS attack?
options: ARP messages flow freely through switches.
explanation: ARP performs no authentication, so any device can send ARP replies with false IP-to-MAC mappings. Hosts accept these replies and update their ARP tables, which lets an attacker poison them. Poisoned tables can redirect or drop traffic, causing an on-path attack or a DoS attack.
whyWrong: ARP does not use passwords, so hashing is not involved.
ARP messages are broadcast within the local network, but this is not what makes ARP open to abuse.
ARP tables can be changed, but the weakness is that ARP accepts changes without checking who sent them.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 10: Risk Management, Review Questions question 10

stem: A company accidentally sends a newsletter with a mistyped website address. The address points to a website that has been spoofed by hackers to collect information from people who make the same typo. What kind of attack is this?
explanation: A spoofed website that collects information from people who mistype an address is a form of phishing. Phishing uses communication or sites that appear legitimate to trick people into giving up information. This specific technique, which relies on a typo in a domain name, is also called typosquatting.
whyWrong: Tailgating is following an authorized person through a secured door.
Quid pro quo offers the victim something in exchange for information or access.
Baiting leaves an infected file or device for the victim to pick up and use.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 10: Risk Management, Scenario-Based Questions question 1
note: The book gives no answer; this attack is typosquatting, and phishing is the closest listed type.

stem: Your organization has just approved a special budget for a network security upgrade. What procedure should you conduct to develop your recommendations for the upgrade priorities?
explanation: A posture assessment is a thorough examination of each part of the network to find how it might be compromised. Its results show where the greatest risks are, so they help set priorities for a security upgrade. A security audit, by contrast, checks the organization against a set standard.
whyWrong: A data breach is unauthorized access to sensitive data, not a procedure you conduct.
A security audit checks compliance with a standard rather than examining every way the network could be compromised.
An exploit is the act of taking advantage of a vulnerability, not a planning procedure.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 10: Risk Management, Scenario-Based Questions question 2
note: N10-009 does not list assessment types; audits and compliance is the closest topic.

stem: A former employee discovers six months after they start work at a new company that their account credentials still give them access to their old company’s servers. They demonstrate their access to several friends to brag about their cleverness and talk badly about the company. What kind of attack is this?
explanation: An insider threat comes from someone who has or had authorized access, such as a current or former employee. Here the former employee still has working credentials and uses them to access the old company's servers. Off-boarding should disable accounts when employees leave to prevent this threat.
whyWrong: The principle of least privilege is a security practice, not an attack.
A vulnerability is a weakness, while the question asks about the attack of a person who misuses access.
A denial of service makes resources unavailable, but the former employee is accessing the servers.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 10: Risk Management, Scenario-Based Questions question 3

stem: A neighbor hacks into your secured wireless network on a regular basis, but you didn’t give her the password. What loophole was MOST LIKELY left open?
options: The firmware contains a back door.
The default password was not changed.
The router has been recruited by a botnet.
Her network is using the same credentials as yours.
explanation: Default administrative passwords for wireless routers are widely published, so anyone in range can sign in if they were not changed. An attacker with administrative access can read or change the wireless settings and keep getting in. Changing default passwords is a basic step in device hardening.
whyWrong: A firmware back door is possible but much less likely than an unchanged default password.
A router in a botnet is used to attack others and does not explain how the neighbor joins the network.
Neighbors using the same credentials by chance is very unlikely and is not a loophole left open on your network.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 10: Risk Management, Scenario-Based Questions question 4

stem: What kind of software can be used to secure employee-owned devices?
explanation: Mobile device configurations can be handled automatically by MDM (mobile device management) software, which increases BYOD (bring your own device) security by ensuring that employee-owned devices conform to company-defined security policies. An AUP (acceptable use policy) explains to users what they can and cannot do while accessing a network's resources. An NDA (non-disclosure agreement) defines what information an organization identifies as confidential and private and how that information should be protected.
whyWrong: An AUP is a policy that tells users what they can and cannot do on the network, not software.
An NDA is an agreement about protecting confidential information, not software.
BYOD is the practice of using employee-owned devices, not the software that secures them.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 11: Access Control, Self-Check question 1

stem: Which of the following is more of a detective security technology than a preventive technology?
explanation: A detective security technology is primarily intended to identify a breach that has occurred rather than preventing the breach in the first place. Although security cameras can be a deterrent to crime, their primary use is to alert when a breach occurs and then to provide information about the breach after it has occurred. Smart lockers, cipher locks, and access badge readers can sometimes be designed to detect a breach as it occurs; however, these technologies are primarily intended to prevent the breach in the first place.
whyWrong: A smart locker is mainly a preventive control that keeps items locked away.
A cipher lock is mainly a preventive control that keeps a door locked.
An access badge is mainly a preventive control that keeps unauthorized people out.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 11: Access Control, Self-Check question 2

stem: Which access control technique is responsible for detection of an intruder who succeeds in accessing a network?
explanation: The accounting system logs users’ access and activities on the network and can be used to detect illicit activity on a network. In other words, accounting asks, “What did you do?” Authentication is the process of verifying a user’s credentials to grant the user access to secured resources on a system or network. Geofencing determines a client’s geographic location to enforce a virtual security perimeter. SoD (separation of duties) refers to the division of labor such that no one person can singlehandedly compromise the security of data, finances, or other resources.
whyWrong: Authentication verifies credentials before access is granted, so it does not detect what an intruder does afterward.
Geofencing uses a client's location to enforce a virtual security perimeter.
Separation of duties divides tasks so no one person can compromise security alone.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 11: Access Control, Self-Check question 3

stem: Which authorization method will allow Nancy, a custodian, to access the company’s email application but not its accounting system?
explanation: With RBAC (role-based access control), a network administrator creates user groups associated with job roles and assigns privileges and permissions to each role. Each user is assigned to a user group that matches a requirement for their job. With DAC (discretionary access control), users decide for themselves who has access to that user’s resources. In the context of AAA, auditing refers to checking user configurations for problems, searching for signs of account misuse, and monitoring a network for compromised accounts. Local authentication processes are performed on a single device.
whyWrong: Auditing checks accounts and activity for misuse and does not grant access.
With DAC, users decide who can access their own resources, rather than access being based on a job role.
Local authentication checks credentials on a single device and does not assign permissions by role.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 11: Access Control, Self-Check question 4

stem: Which authentication protocol is optimized for wireless clients?
explanation: Due to its origins as a remote authentication service, RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) specializes in supporting clients not directly wired into the network, such as clients of wireless access points or VPN-based clients. While Active Directory offers powerful authentication and other services, it's limited to working with Windows or Linux clients, and it can't directly support authentication through wireless access points. TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access Control System Plus) is most often used for device administration access control for technicians. Kerberos is a cross-platform authentication protocol that uses key encryption to verify the identity of clients.
whyWrong: Active Directory cannot directly support authentication through wireless access points.
TACACS+ is mostly used to control administrative access to network devices.
Kerberos is a cross-platform protocol that uses tickets and keys, not one built for wireless clients.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 11: Access Control, Self-Check question 5

stem: What does a client present to a network server to access a resource on that server?
explanation: A ticket is a temporary set of credentials a client presents to network servers to prove its identity has been validated. A key belongs to the client or server and is used to initially validate their respective identities to each other during the authentication process to create a session. A principal is a Kerberos client or user. A TGT (Ticket-Granting Ticket) will expire within a specified amount of time and is used to request tickets in order to gain access to network services.
whyWrong: A key validates the client or server to the authentication service, but it is not what the client shows to a resource server.
A principal is a Kerberos client or user, not a credential.
A ticket-granting ticket is used to request tickets from the ticket-granting service, not to access a resource server.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 11: Access Control, Self-Check question 6

stem: When you use your Microsoft credentials to sign into an app on your phone, what is responsible for defining the terms of communication between your phone and Microsoft?
explanation: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) is a standard that defines the rules of communication and secure authentication processes between an IdP (identity provider) and an SP (service provider). Although AD could be considered an IdP, it is not the standard used to define communications between an IdP and an SP.
whyWrong: The IdP authenticates the user and stores credentials but does not define the communication rules.
The SP is the application that relies on the IdP, not the standard for their communication.
Active Directory could act as an identity store but is not the standard used between an IdP and an SP.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 11: Access Control, Self-Check question 7

stem: Which principle ensures auditing processes are managed by someone other than the employees whose activities are being audited?
explanation: Separation of duties divides tasks so that no single person can compromise security alone. Having someone other than the audited employees manage the auditing process applies this principle. It keeps people from hiding their own misuse of the systems they work on.
whyWrong: Least privilege gives users only the access they need for their job, not separate people for auditing.
The shared responsibility model divides security duties between a cloud provider and its customer.
Defense in depth uses many layers of security controls to protect resources.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 11: Access Control, Review Questions question 1
note: Separation of duties is not named in N10-009 4.1; it is closest to authorization.

stem: Active Directory and 389 Directory Server are both compatible with which directory access protocol?
explanation: AD (Active Directory), OpenLDAP, and 389 Directory Server are all built to be LDAP-compliant. LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is the standard protocol for accessing and querying a directory. LDAPS adds SSL/TLS encryption and uses port 636.
whyWrong: AD DS is the Active Directory service itself, not a directory access protocol.
Kerberos is an authentication protocol, not the protocol used to access a directory.
RADIUS is a AAA protocol for remote and wireless users, not a directory access protocol.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 11: Access Control, Review Questions question 2

stem: Which of the following is the most important factor when designing a strong password?
explanation: Length is the most important factor in a strong password, because a longer password is much harder to crack by brute force, regardless of its complexity. Current advice is at least 15 characters for low-sensitivity accounts and more for sensitive ones. Complexity helps too, but long is strong.
whyWrong: A familiar password is easier for an attacker to guess.
Complexity helps, but a short complex password is still weaker against brute force than a long one.
Memorability makes a password easier to use but does not make it stronger.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 11: Access Control, Review Questions question 3

stem: What feature on a firewall can block malicious email traffic?
explanation: Content filtering examines the actual content of messages, including email traffic, and blocks what is malicious or not allowed. It can detect illegal content, contact with malicious sites, and software that exploits known weaknesses. URL filtering works only from a list of allowed or blocked web addresses.
whyWrong: URL filtering blocks or allows web addresses from a list and does not inspect email content.
Aggregation combines links or data and is not a firewall filtering feature.
Hashing checks data integrity and does not filter email traffic.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 11: Access Control, Review Questions question 4

stem: What technology can be used to increase BYOD security?
explanation: MDM (mobile device management) software manages and secures mobile devices, including employee-owned ones. It makes BYOD devices meet company security policies and can remotely wipe a lost device. This makes it the main technology for improving BYOD security.
whyWrong: An NDA is an agreement that protects confidential information, not a technology.
IAM manages user identities and access in general rather than the security of employee-owned devices.
Separation of duties divides tasks among people and does not secure devices.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 11: Access Control, Review Questions question 5

stem: Which part of AAA is MOST LIKELY to rely on encryption keys as an integral part of the process?
explanation: Authentication protocols such as Kerberos use encryption keys to verify the identity of clients and servers. The keys prove identity without sending the password itself across the network. Authorization and accounting work after identity has been established.
whyWrong: Authorization decides what a user can do after authentication and does not depend on encryption keys.
Accounting logs what users do on the network and does not depend on encryption keys.
Auditing reviews accounts and activity for misuse and is not the AAA step that relies on keys.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 11: Access Control, Review Questions question 6

stem: Which of the following combinations of information is an example of MFA?
explanation: MFA requires factors from two or more different categories. A birthdate is something you know, and a fingerprint is something you are, so together they are MFA. The other pairs combine two items from the same category.
whyWrong: A voice pattern and a typing style are both something you do, so they are one factor type.
A password and a PIN are both something you know, so they are one factor type.
A smart card and a key are both something you have, so they are one factor type.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 11: Access Control, Review Questions question 7

stem: Which of these technologies should be used to authenticate a network technician to a Cisco router?
explanation: TACACS+ is a Cisco-developed AAA protocol that is typically used to authenticate technicians to network devices such as routers and switches. It runs over TCP and encrypts all AAA information. It also lets administrators separate authentication, authorization, and accounting.
whyWrong: Active Directory authenticates users and computers in a Windows domain, not technicians on routers.
SAML defines communication between an identity provider and a service provider for web and cloud applications.
RADIUS mostly authenticates remote and wireless users and encrypts only the password.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 11: Access Control, Review Questions question 8

stem: Which of the following statements about SAML is false?
options: An SP does not need to store user passwords.
An SP can require users to rotate their passwords on a certain schedule.
An IdP sends an authentication token to the SP.
explanation: With SAML, the IdP stores the user's credentials and sends an authentication token to the SP. Because the SP never stores the passwords, it cannot require users to rotate them. Password rules and MFA are enforced by the IdP.
whyWrong: This statement is true, because the IdP stores the credentials and the SP does not.
This statement is true, because the IdP authenticates the user and can require MFA.
This statement is true, because the IdP sends a token to the SP after authentication.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 11: Access Control, Review Questions question 9

stem: You’re doing an audit of your company’s user accounts, permissions, and job roles. A help-desk technician needs to be able to reset user passwords, as this is the most common issue reported in troubleshooting tickets. Which of the following permissions should the technician be given to do their job?
explanation: Under the principle of least privilege, the technician gets only the permission needed to do the job. Resetting a password means setting a new one, so the create password permission covers the task. Creating or deleting users is more access than the job requires.
whyWrong: Listing passwords does not let the technician set a new password and would expose sensitive data.
Creating users is more access than resetting passwords requires.
Deleting users is more access than resetting passwords requires.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 11: Access Control, Scenario-Based Questions question 2

stem: Which of the following standards describes a security technique, often used on wireless networks, in which a port is prevented from receiving traffic until the transmitter’s credentials are verified by an authentication server?
explanation: EAPoL (EAP over LAN) is defined by IEEE 802.1X, which keeps a port from passing traffic until the device's credentials are verified.
